strengths: Compelling conceptual grounding connecting cognitive science, information theory (the Information Bottleneck principle), and the study of inductive biases in LLMs.

Clever adaptation of the iterated language learning (ILL) paradigm into iterated in-context language learning (IICLL) using pseudowords, which effectively prevents the models from simply retrieving known natural language color terms.
Interesting empirical results showing that LLMs (Gemini and Llama) iteratively evolve random pseudo-color assignments toward the IB efficiency frontier and human-like categorization systems.
Thoughtful comparison between textual sRGB input representations and multimodal visual inputs.
weaknesses: The manuscript appears unfinished and lacks key experimental details: there are broken citation markers in the text (e.g., '[? ]' on page 2 and page 4) and typographical errors (e.g., '1 Introducton').

Missing procedural specifications: the paper does not specify essential experimental hyperparameters, such as the exact prompts used, decoding parameters (temperature, top-p), the sample size of color-pseudoword pairs presented in context ($d_{t-1}$), the number of parallel chains run, and how variance across seeds was controlled.

Limited model exploration: only two models (Gemini 2.0-flash and Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct) are evaluated. The paper attributes Llama's lower complexity to model size ('the smaller model'), but this claim is unsubstantiated without comparing model families across systematic parameter scales (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B vs. 70B vs. 405B).

Superficial discussion of the underlying mechanism: it remains unclear whether the observed bias stems from the geometry of the input representations (e.g., proximity in RGB/vision encoder space), the statistical properties of human language encountered during pre-training, or inherent properties of in-context learning.

strengths: The paper addresses a compelling and fundamental interdisciplinary question: whether large language models exhibit human-like inductive biases toward efficient semantic compression as characterized by the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle.
Grounding the investigation in established cognitive science paradigms—specifically the World Color Survey (WCS) framework and iterated learning—provides a solid theoretical foundation.
The adaptation of iterated in-context learning to color category systems (IICLL) is an interesting conceptual approach to probing inductive biases in language models.
The comparison between textual representations (RGB coordinates) and direct visual inputs (image patches) offers useful preliminary insight into modality-dependent inductive biases.
weaknesses: The manuscript appears unfinished and lacks crucial technical and implementation details: there are broken citation placeholders ('[? ]' appears on pages 2 and 4), typographical errors in major section headers ('1 Introducton'), and the text is only 4 pages long, omitting essential methodological depth.

The experimental setup is underspecified. Key experimental parameters are missing or inadequately detailed, including exact prompt formulations, sampling size of the subset $d_{t-1}$, sampling temperature, generation lengths, and chain termination criteria.
The formal mathematical definitions of the core evaluation metrics ('efficiency loss', 'IB-alignment', and 'human-alignment') are not explicitly provided in the text.

The evaluation is restricted to only two models (Gemini 2.0-flash and Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct). Testing across a broader range of model families, sizes, and open-source vision-language architectures would be necessary to substantiate general claims about LLM inductive biases.
Figure 1 is overcrowded, and sub-panels (especially 1F, 1G, and 1H) have extremely small axis text and legends that are difficult to read.

Potential confounders in the iterated in-context learning setup are insufficiently explored. For example, it is unclear to what degree the convergence towards smooth partitions is driven by perceptual priors versus contextual drift, token frequency biases, or decoding dynamics.

strengths: Compelling theoretical grounding: Connecting LLM in-context learning and semantic organization to the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle and iterated learning literature (e.g., Zaslavsky et al., Xu et al.) is conceptually elegant and cognitively well-motivated.

Interesting experimental paradigm: Adapting iterated learning to in-context LLM generations (IICLL) using pseudowords effectively controls for direct surface-level memorization of English color terms, allowing a cleaner test of inductive biases.

Clear and informative visualizations: Figure 1 effectively illustrates the experimental pipeline, empirical results on the information plane, and convergence dynamics toward human and IB optima across generations.
weaknesses: Missing citations and proofreading issues: There are uncompiled citation placeholders (`[? ]`) on page 2 and page 4 when referring to the iterated in-context learning paradigm.

Lack of critical implementation details: The paper omits key experimental hyperparameters, including the specific prompt templates used, sampling settings (temperature, top-p), the exact size of the sampled subset $d_{t-1}$ presented in-context, and how many chains were run per condition.

Limited model exploration: The study tests only two models (Gemini 2.0-flash and Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct). While the authors mention other open models struggled, evaluating additional leading models (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, or Qwen 2.5) would establish whether these findings generalize across architectures and training paradigms.

Assumptions regarding perceptual space: The communicative accuracy and perceptual noise model rely on human CIELAB space. While justified when evaluating alignment with human semantics, the paper does not thoroughly discuss whether the LLM's internal representation of colors (especially via RGB text inputs) reflects non-Euclidean perceptual geometries.

strengths: Grounding in cognitive science and information theory: The paper connects the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle of human semantic categorization (Zaslavsky et al., 2018) with iterated learning in LLMs, providing a theoretically principled framework to assess semantic compression and inductive biases.

Comprehensive empirical scope: The English naming study benchmarks an extensive suite of 39 models across 6 families, varying in scale, modality, and post-training stages, which provides clear insights into the emergence of semantic structure with scale and instruction tuning.

Methodological rigor in IICLL: The Iterated In-Context Language Learning setup carefully isolates inductive bias by using nonsense labels and abstract feature representations (without explicitly mentioning 'color'). The inclusion of rotation analyses and nearest-neighbor baselines effectively rules out trivial geometric clustering or arbitrary coordinate memorization.

Clear insights into emergent capabilities: The paper demonstrates a compelling phenomenon where models iteratively compress and restructure random category mappings toward the theoretical IB frontier, mimicking human cultural evolution dynamics.
weaknesses: Disparity across models and reliance on Gemini 2.0: While the theoretical narrative is compelling, only Gemini 2.0 successfully spans the full range of human-like IB trade-offs, whereas leading open-weight models (e.g., Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 32B) collapse into lower-complexity or degenerate systems. The proprietary and closed nature of Gemini makes it difficult to disentangle whether this is driven by RLHF/system prompting, tokenization advantages, or genuine in-context reasoning capacity.

Sensitivity to input representation: The authors observe that while sRGB triples work well, CIELAB coordinates lead to degraded performance across all models. Given that CIELAB is perceptually uniform, this divergence suggests that performance may be heavily tied to how frequently sRGB numbers appear alongside color terms in web pretraining data rather than a purely perceptual grounding.

Heuristic sliding window implementation: Generalization in IICLL relies on a sliding conversation window of the 10 most recent predictions to avoid degenerate collapse. While motivated by human working memory, this architectural heuristic introduces sequential dependencies that could influence the stationary distribution of the Markov chain.

strengths: Grounding in cognitive science theory: The paper successfully bridges the Information Bottleneck (IB) framework of semantic compression (Zaslavsky et al.) with iterated learning (Kirby, Griffiths) to study the inductive biases of LLMs in semantic categorization.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate 39 models across 6 model families (Gemini, Gemma, Llama, Qwen, OLMo, GPT-2), spanning multiple scales, instruction-tuned vs. base variants, training checkpoints, and text vs. vision modalities.

Principled experimental methodology: The Iterated In-Context Language Learning (IICLL) protocol is carefully designed and includes important sanity checks, such as training set comprehension checks, rotation analysis along the hue dimension to rule out trivial partition artifacts, and comparison against a nearest-neighbor baseline.

Clear presentation and relevance: The paper is well-written, structured logically, and addresses an important question regarding how LLMs compress and organize semantic concepts relative to human cognitive efficiency.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a closed proprietary model for key claims: While the authors find that LLMs generally restructure categories toward IB efficiency, only Gemini 2.0 successfully recapitulates the full range of complexity-accuracy tradeoffs (such as higher k values), whereas the best open-weight models (Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 2.5 32B) converge primarily to low-complexity systems. Because Gemini 2.0 is closed-source with unknown pretraining data and alignment recipes, it is hard to disentangle intrinsic model inductive biases from specific training data contamination.

Representation sensitivity: As shown in Appendix C, models perform poorly when presented with CIELAB coordinates compared to sRGB triples, despite CIELAB being a more perceptually uniform space. This sensitivity suggests that model behavior is heavily mediated by the frequent occurrence of sRGB/hex color codes in web training corpora rather than a domain-general perceptual abstraction.

Limited evaluation outside the color domain: The overarching claim focuses on human-aligned categorization broadly, but the empirical support rests almost exclusively on the color domain. The exploration of Shepard circles in Section 4.3 is preliminary, restricted only to Gemini with images, and lacks the quantitative depth of the color experiments.

Heuristic modifications in the IICLL protocol: The use of an ad-hoc 10-turn sliding conversational history window during generation was required to prevent degenerate collapses (Appendix K). While justified pragmatically, this introduces an additional autoregressive dependence that complicates the theoretical mapping to standard Bayesian iterated learning.

strengths: Fascinating and principled theoretical bridge combining cognitive science frameworks (the Information Bottleneck principle of semantic compression and iterated learning) with the behavioral study of large language models.

Comprehensive empirical scope across 39 language models from 6 model families, exploring the effects of model scale, base vs. instruction tuning, text vs. multimodal inputs, and pretraining checkpoints (OLMo 2).

Methodologically sound experiment design with Iterated In-Context Language Learning (IICLL); using nonsense pseudo-words and abstract feature vectors ensures that the observed convergence toward IB-efficiency cannot simply be attributed to direct memorization of English color labels.

Thorough evaluation and controls, including the rotation analysis (Appendix H) verifying non-trivial perceptual alignment with the World Color Survey (WCS), comparison against a nearest-neighbor baseline (Appendix M), and window-size ablations (Appendix K).
weaknesses: The core finding that LLMs can recapitulate the full range of human-like IB trade-offs across higher category granularities ($k$ up to 14) relies heavily on a single closed-source proprietary model (Gemini 2.0 Flash); all open-weight models tested (e.g., Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 2.5 32B, Gemma 3 27B) collapse or converge only to low-complexity systems.

Sensitivity to input representation: As demonstrated in Appendix C, models degrade significantly when prompted with perceptually uniform CIELAB coordinates instead of sRGB values. This suggests that the models' inductive biases remain strongly coupled to digital/textual co-occurrence statistics of sRGB values rather than an invariant conceptual representation.

The extension beyond color (Shepard circles, Section 4.3) is very preliminary, qualitative, and restricted to only Gemini 2.0 with image inputs, leaving the claim of domain generality largely unproven.
